title: The Monsoon Just Arrived Three Days Late. The Forecast Behind It Is the Worst India Has Seen in 11 Years.
excerpt: IMD puts the chance of a deficient monsoon at 60 percent as El Niño strengthens, colliding with an oil shock and a weakening rupee to create the tightest squeeze Indian farmers have faced this decade.
body:
The monsoon reached Kerala on Thursday, three days behind its usual June 1 arrival, offering the first hint of relief from a heatwave that had pushed power demand to record highs. But the late onset is the least of India's worries. The India Meteorological Department's latest forecast suggests this could be the weakest monsoon season in more than a decade, arriving just as the economy can least afford it.

## The Numbers Are Stark

IMD revised its seasonal forecast downward on May 29, projecting rainfall at just 90 percent of the Long Period Average — down from 92 percent in its April estimate and right at the threshold of what qualifies as a deficient season. The probability table is more alarming: there is a 60 percent chance of deficient rainfall and a 24 percent chance of below-normal rainfall. Together, that means an 84 percent probability that the monsoon will underperform.

The culprit is El Niño, which the World Meteorological Organization now says could be strong. El Niño warms the equatorial Pacific, disrupting the wind and pressure systems that pull moisture from the Indian Ocean toward the subcontinent. Historically, around 60 percent of El Niño years have produced deficient rainfall in India. The Indian Ocean Dipole, which can sometimes offset El Niño's damage, is expected to remain neutral — removing one of India's most reliable weather buffers.

## What This Means for Farmers and Food Prices

The monsoon delivers nearly 70 percent of India's annual rainfall and is the single most important variable for the country's $4 trillion economy. It determines whether farmers can plant rice, soybeans, pulses, cotton, sugarcane, and corn on time — and whether the 45 percent of the workforce that depends on agriculture will earn enough to sustain rural demand.

The regional picture adds another layer of concern. IMD expects below-normal rainfall over Central India, South Peninsular India, and Northwest India — regions that grow a large share of the country's rain-fed pulses, oilseeds, and coarse cereals. The Monsoon Core Zone, which covers much of India's rainfed agriculture belt, is also expected to see below-normal rainfall.

Dry pre-monsoon soils compound the risk. When the topsoil enters June parched, the first rains are absorbed before they can sustain a germinating crop. Agricultural experts warn that uneven distribution could pose a bigger challenge than the headline deficit number suggests.

## The Macro Collision

This would be hard enough in a normal year. In 2026, it collides with an oil shock that has already pushed inflation higher and weakened the rupee by more than 5 percent since January. The Reserve Bank of India, which announces its rate decision on Friday, faces the prospect of food prices rising at the same time energy costs remain elevated — the kind of twin pressure that constrains every policy option.

A weak monsoon typically feeds through to higher food inflation within two to three months, as kharif crop output falls short and wholesale prices adjust. Madan Sabnavis, Chief Economist at Bank of Baroda, has noted that the IMD forecast, combined with geopolitical tensions, is "not favourable for inflation," particularly when it has already come in at 3.4 percent in March and is expected to average around 4.6 percent in the current fiscal year.

## The Signal for Rural India

If the monsoon underperforms as projected, the impact will ripple beyond agriculture. Drinking water crises could emerge in rural areas, forcing more extraction of groundwater and contamination of rivers and lakes. Rural consumption — which had shown signs of recovering after two years of decent monsoon seasons — could weaken again, dragging growth in sectors from FMCG to two-wheelers.

For the Indian diaspora watching from abroad, the monsoon is not just a weather event. It is the single largest economic variable their families back home face every year, and this year it arrives under a cloud of compounding risks.
